title: Mughal Empire
wiki_lead:
The Mughal Empire was an early modern empire in South Asia. At its peak, the empire stretched from the outer fringes of the Indus River Basin in the west, northern Afghanistan in the northwest, and Kashmir in the north, to the highlands of present-day Assam and Bangladesh in the east, and the uplands of the Deccan Plateau in South India.
The Mughal Empire is conventionally said to have been founded in 1526 by Babur, a Timurid prince hailing from the Fergana Valley in Central Asia, who, with assistance from the Safavid and Ottoman empires, defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, in the First Battle of Panipat and swept down the plains of northern India. The Mughal imperial structure, however, is sometimes dated to 1600, during the rule of Babur's grandson, Akbar. This imperial structure lasted until 1720, shortly after the death of the last major emperor, Aurangzeb, during whose reign the empire also achieved its maximum geographical extent. Reduced subsequently to the region in and around Old Delhi by 1760, the empire was formally dissolved by the British Raj after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
Although the Mughal Empire was created and sustained by military warfare, it did not vigorously suppress the cultures and peoples it came to rule; rather, it equalised and placated them through new administrative practices, and diverse ruling elites, leading to more efficient, centralised, and standardised rule. The basis of the empire's collective wealth was agricultural taxes, implemented by the third Mughal emperor, Akbar. These taxes, which amounted to well over half the output of a peasant cultivator, were paid in a well-regulated silver currency, and allowed peasants and artisans to enter larger markets.
The relative peace maintained by the empire during much of the 17th century was a factor in India's economic expansion. The burgeoning European presence in the Indian Ocean and an increasing demand for Indian raw and finished products generated much wealth for the Mughal court. There was conspicuous consumption among the Mughal elite, resulting in greater patronage of painting, literary forms, textiles, and architecture, especially during the reign of Shah Jahan. Among the Mughal UNESCO World Heritage Sites in South Asia are Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Lahore Fort, Shalamar Gardens, and the Taj Mahal, which has been described as "the jewel of Muslim art in India, and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage".

Name
The word Mughal (also spelled Mogul or Moghul in English) is the Indo-Persian form of Mongol, used in India to highlight its rulers' Turco-Mongol origins, and to set them apart from the Afghan elite who ruled the Delhi Sultanate. In the West, the terms Grand Mughal and Mughal were used for the emperor and, by extension, the empire as a whole.
The closest to an official name for the empire was Hindustan, which was documented in the Ain-i-Akbari. Mughal administrative records also refer to the empire as "dominion of Hindustan" (Wilāyat-i-Hindustān), "country of Hind" (Bilād-i-Hind), "Sultanate of al-Hind" (Salṭanat(i) al-Hindīyyah), as observed in the epitaph of Emperor Aurangzeb, or endonymous identification from emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as "Land of Hind" (Hindostān) in Hindustani. Contemporary Chinese chronicles referred to the empire as Hindustan (Héndūsītǎn). The Hindu kings of Nepal pejoratively referred to the Mughal Empire as Mughlana, in contrast with their own kingdom, which they referred to as Asal Hindustan (lit. 'real land of the Hindus'). 
The term "Mughal Dynasty" remains disputed by Indologists. In Marshall Hodgson's view, a better historiographical designation would be Timurid/Timuri or Indo-Timurid. Members of the dynasty called it Gurkani (Gūrkāniyān), a reference to their descent from the Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur, who took the title Gūrkān 'son-in-law' after his marriage to a Chinggisid princess.


History


Babur and Humayun (1526–1556)

The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur (reigned 1526–1530), a Central Asian ruler who was descended from the Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur (the founder of the Timurid Empire) on his father's side, and from Genghis Khan on his mother's side. Paternally, Babur belonged to the Turkified Barlas tribe of Mongol origin. Ousted from his ancestral domains in Central Asia, Babur turned to India to satisfy his ambitions. He established himself in Kabul and then pushed steadily southward into India from Afghanistan through the Khyber Pass. Babur's forces defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. Through his use of firearms and cannons, he was able to shatter Ibrahim's armies despite being at a numerical disadvantage, expanding his dominion up to the mid Indo-Gangetic Plain. After the battle, the centre of Mughal power shifted to Agra. The Battle of Khanwa fought near Agra in 1527 between Babur and Rana Sanga of Mewar was another decisive victory in the Mughal conquest of northern India.
The preoccupation with wars and military campaigns, however, did not allow the new emperor to consolidate the gains he had made in India. The instability of the empire became evident under his son, Humayun (reigned 1530–1556), who was forced into exile in Persia by the rebellious Sher Shah Suri (reigned 1540–1545). Humayun's exile in Persia established diplomatic ties between the Safavid and Mughal courts and led to increasing Persian cultural influence in the later restored Mughal Empire. Humayun's triumphant return from Persia in 1555 restored Mughal rule in some parts of India, but he died in an accident the next year.


Akbar to Aurangzeb (1556–1707)

grok_lead: The Mughal Empire was a Turco-Mongol Muslim dynasty that ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from its founding in 1526 until its effective dissolution in 1857. Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, established the empire after defeating Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of the Delhi Sultanate at the First Battle of Panipat on April 21, 1526, using superior artillery and tactics despite being outnumbered. The empire expanded through military conquests and strategic alliances, notably with Hindu Rajput states such as the Kingdom of Amber, the Kingdom of Bikaner, and the Kingdom of Jaisalmer, including matrimonial ties with Hindu Rajput clans such as the Kachwahas, Rathores, and Bhattis, through which later Mughal rulers became increasingly Indian Rajput on their maternal side. This incorporated diverse Hindu-majority populations under a centralized administration that emphasized Turkic-led Persianate culture, which evolved into Indo-Persianate culture by mixing elements of Indian and Persianate cultures, along with land revenue extraction and a mansabdari ranking system for nobles. Under emperors like Akbar (r. 1556â1605), the empire consolidated power via administrative reforms, including a tolerant religious policy of sulh-i-kul (universal peace) that abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims and promoted syncretic ideas like Din-i Ilahi, fostering relative stability and cultural flourishing in arts, architecture, and trade. However, later rulers such as Aurangzeb (r. 1658â1707) shifted to stricter orthodox Islamic policies, reimposing jizya, enforcing Sharia, and destroying Hindu temples, which alienated large segments of the non-Muslim population and fueled rebellions among Hindu Marathas, Punjabi Sikhs, Hindu Jats, and Hindu Rajputs. At its zenith under Aurangzeb, the empire spanned nearly the entire subcontinent, from Afghanistan to the Deccan, but prolonged Deccan wars overstretched resources, exacerbating jagirdari crises where land assignments failed to cover military obligations. The empire's decline accelerated after Aurangzeb's death in 1707 due to weak successors, succession wars, economic stagnation from high taxation and agrarian exploitation, and the rise of regional powers. Delhi was repeatedly targeted: by the Marathas in 1737, by Turcoman warrior Nader Shah in 1739, by the Jats under Suraj Mal in 1753, and by the Sikh Misls (1766â1788). By the mid-eighteenth century, Mughal control over Delhi was only nominal. From 1771 to 1803, roughly three decades, the Maratha Empire held effective control of Delhi and kept the emperor under their protection. The empire formally ended in 1857 when the British East India Company deposed the last emperor, Bahadur Shah II, following the Indian Rebellion. Despite achievements in monumental architecture like the Taj Mahal and a sophisticated revenue system that generated vast wealth, the Mughal polity's reliance on coercive extraction and failure to adapt to fiscal-military challengesârather than any inherent cultural superiorityâultimately led to its fragmentation amid European colonial incursions. Scholarly assessments, often influenced by institutional biases favoring narratives of syncretism over conquest dynamics, underemphasize how religious impositions and endless warfare eroded legitimacy among subject populations.
